01 · Overview

About this dashboard

THE QUESTION THIS DASHBOARD ANSWERS
America is investing billions to build its emerging-tech workforce — computer chips, artificial intelligence, biotechnology. Are those dollars reaching the colleges already producing nearly 1 in 3 of the nation's STEM graduates? HBCUs and MSIs produce 30.7% of America's STEM bachelor's degrees but hold just 8.3% of the nation's academic research funding.
STEM DEGREES PRODUCED
30.7%
of U.S. STEM bachelor's degrees, 2022
FEDERAL R&D RECEIVED
8.3%
of NSF HERD total, FY2023 ($9.0B of $108.7B)
The pipeline is real. The federal infrastructure to channel its graduates into national-priority research careers is not. At the current pace, doubling the MSI share of federal STEM production would take ~54 years. Federal investments like the CHIPS Act are designed to accelerate this — but only if the colleges producing the graduates have the research funding to compete for the grants.

READ FIRST Methodology & Limits — how to read these numbers ▾

Every claim in this dashboard is traceable to source data — but the framing matters. Five things worth knowing before you cite these numbers:

1. The "1 in 3" / 30.7% MSI share is bachelor's-level only, federal STEM scope.
Numerator: 553 CIPs from the NCES STEM list (513) + DHS STEM-Designated Degree Program List (40 additional, including military and pharmaceutical sciences). Denominator: NCES Digest Table 318.45 bachelor's STEM total (NCES 513-CIP scope). The apples-to-apples NCES-only figure is 30.43%; the federal-scope figure (NCES+DHS) is 30.70%. Both tell the same story.
2. The "8 cents on the dollar" is share of NSF HERD-frame R&D — not all federal STEM funding.
NSF HERD covers institutions that grant bachelor's+ and expend ≥$150K/yr on R&D. The 654 MSIs outside the HERD frame still receive federal funds (Title III, SIP, NSF HBCU-UP and HRD programs, USDA Capacity Building, etc.) that this denominator does not include. Reading: "Of NSF-surveyed academic R&D, MSIs receive 8.3% — and the institutional R&D capacity needed to compete for CHIPS/NSTC R&D dollars is concentrated outside the MSI sector."
3. Federal priority-area counts are a FLOOR, not a ceiling.
The alignment between academic programs and priority areas is deliberately conservative: only programs whose name explicitly references the priority area are counted. A Computer Science grad doing quantum software won't be credited to Quantum; a Biology grad working in semiconductors won't show up in Semiconductors. Counts reflect "graduates from programs explicitly named for this priority." True workforce contribution is higher but cannot be measured at national scale without administrative wage record linkage.
4. The demographic × priority matrix shows representation, not causation.
A red cell means "this race group is a smaller share of MSI graduates in this priority area than they are in MSI STEM overall" — a representation gap. It is NOT a claim that these students cannot succeed in these fields, or that their MSIs are at fault. The mechanisms driving the gap (lab infrastructure, faculty pipelines, federal grant access) are visible in the R&D Capacity section, and the federal CHIPS/NSTC authorities exist to address them.
5. 24 of 772 institutions have incomplete 10-year coverage.
Mostly newly-opened institutions (founded 2014+), branch campuses with separate IPEDS UNITID histories starting later, or institutions that closed (e.g., Morris Brown College reopened 2022). The full list is in downloads/01_institution_roster.csv's trend_coverage column. National totals weight by years-reported, so this doesn't materially affect headline numbers.

Citation: USC STEM Center, "National HBCU & MSI STEM Pipeline Dashboard, v1.0," June 2026. Underlying data from NCES IPEDS (via Urban Institute Education Data Portal), NSF HERD FY2023, U.S. Department of Education OPE Eligibility Matrix (FY2025 + FY2026), CHIPS & Science Act P.L. 117-167, and the NSTC Critical and Emerging Technologies list (Feb 2024). Full methodology in the Methodology & Sources section below.

Data: 10 years of IPEDS completions (2013–2022) joined to NSF HERD (FY2023), NCES Digest national totals, the 19-area CHIPS+NSTC federal STEM priority alignment, and the FY2025/FY2026 OPE Eligibility Matrices. Built for federal funders, policy researchers, higher education leaders, and institutional advocates. All figures traceable to source — see Methodology section.

What is an MSI?

"MSI" (Minority-Serving Institution) is an umbrella term for federally-designated institutions that serve substantial populations of historically underrepresented students. Federal law recognizes seven categories. All institutions in this dashboard hold at least one of these designations under the FY 2025 OPE Eligibility Matrix.

HBCU Historically Black Colleges & Universities Established before 1964 with the principal mission of educating Black Americans. Statutory designation — list maintained by White House Initiative on HBCUs. 100 nationally.
TCCU Tribally Controlled Colleges & Universities Operated by federally recognized tribes under the Tribally Controlled Community College Assistance Act. Statutory designation. 35 nationally.
HSI Hispanic-Serving Institutions Undergraduate enrollment ≥25% Hispanic. Title V eligibility. 518 nationally in FY 2025.
AANAPISI Asian American & Native American Pacific Islander-Serving Institutions Undergraduate enrollment ≥10% AAPI. Title III eligibility. 156 nationally.
PBI Predominantly Black Institutions Undergraduate enrollment ≥40% Black, but not designated HBCU. Title III. 39 nationally.
NASNTI Native American-Serving Nontribal Institutions Undergraduate enrollment ≥10% American Indian / Alaska Native, not tribally controlled. 26 nationally.
ANNH Alaska Native / Native Hawaiian-Serving Institutions Undergraduate enrollment ≥20% Alaska Native or ≥10% Native Hawaiian. 14 nationally.
About the FY 2026 policy shift: Following the December 2025 DOJ legal opinion that race-conscious federal grant eligibility criteria are unconstitutional, the FY 2026 OPE Eligibility Matrix consolidated the traditional MSI categories (HSI / AANAPISI / PBI / NASNTI / ANNH) into a single race-neutral Strengthening Institutions Program (SIP) eligibility test based on financial need and institutional capacity. HBCU and TCCU designations remain unchanged because they are defined by federal statute. This dashboard preserves both frameworks — toggle between FY 2025 and FY 2026 in the Institution Browser to see how each institution's status changed.

AND IN FEDERAL STEM PRIORITY AREAS SPECIFICALLY

Of the 30.7% all-STEM contribution above, a strategically critical share lands in fields explicitly named as CHIPS and NSTC federal STEM priorities — AI, semiconductors, biotech, hypersonics, and 15 more. The counts below are a minimum estimate — a Computer Science grad working on AI isn't counted in AI/ML; a Physics grad working on quantum isn't counted in Quantum. 2013 → 2022. Compared with +62% growth in all MSI STEM bachelor's — priority-field production grew nearly as fast as overall STEM.

Methodology: "Priority fields" = the 64 academic program codes (NCES Classification of Instructional Programs / CIP codes) that explicitly map to one or more of the 19 federal STEM priority areas (CHIPS Key Technology Focus Areas + NSTC Critical & Emerging Technologies). A "minimum estimate" because a graduate from a broader program (e.g., Computer Science, Physics, Electrical Engineering) who works in a priority area isn't credited unless their degree program is explicitly named for that priority. National share comparison (MSI vs. all U.S. in these fields) is on the v1.1 roadmap.

Note: The 2020 cohort reflects COVID-19 disruption to academic-year completions.

EXTERNAL BENCHMARK CHECK
UNCF publishes that HBCUs produce 25% of African American STEM graduates (UNCF Impact Report) — the most-cited benchmark in HBCU policy debates. The 2022 verified calculation from this dashboard: HBCUs alone produce 18.7% of national Black STEM bachelor's (5,589 of 29,917 per NCES Table 318.45 + this dashboard's IPEDS aggregation). Why the gap? UNCF's 25% may be older data, may include all degree levels, or may use a different STEM scope. The combined federally-designated MSI sector — HBCUs, HSIs, AANAPISIs, and other designations — produces 40.1% of national Black STEM bachelor's: HBCUs 18.7% + HSIs 15.9% + other MSIs 5.5%. The combined MSI-sector figure is the most current comprehensive measurement available.

Methodology note: Numerator = MSI bachelor's degrees in 553 federally-defined STEM CIPs (NCES STEM 513 CIPs + DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List 40 CIPs covering specialty military and pharmaceutical sciences). Denominator = NCES Digest Table 318.45 bachelor's STEM total (513-CIP scope). Because the numerator's 40 DHS-only CIPs (~1,200 MSI bachelor's/year) aren't in the denominator, the share is inflated by ~0.3 percentage points. The apples-to-apples NCES-only figure is 30.43% (2022). Both definitions tell the same story: MSIs produce ~30% of U.S. STEM bachelor's.

03 · STEM Production

STEM Production

How MSI production breaks down two ways: by the type of federally-designated institution (HBCU, HSI, TCCU, etc.) and by federal STEM priority area (AI, semiconductors, biotech, hypersonics, etc.).

By Federal Designation

By Federal STEM Priority

Degrees aligned to the 19 unified Federal STEM Priority areas — drawn from the CHIPS & Science Act Key Technology Focus Areas (Congress, 2022) and the NSTC Critical & Emerging Technologies List (National Science & Technology Council, Feb 2024). Each area shows total completions and bachelor's degrees nationally across the 772-school traditional MSI universe. Counts are a floor (narrow CIP attribution) — actual contribution is higher.

Methodology: 12 priority areas appear in both source taxonomies — the well-aligned core (including Disaster Resilience, which maps to CHIPS KTFA 5 and partially to NSTC CET 4). The remaining 7 are NSTC-only (specialized national-security technologies: Gas Turbine, Sensing/Signature Mgmt, Directed Energy, Human-Machine Interfaces, Hypersonics, PNT, and Space Tech). Total: 12 + 7 = 19 unified priority areas. CIP-to-priority mapping is researcher-derived, citing both the CHIPS Act text (Section 10387) and the named technology areas in the NSTC CET 2024 list. No federal source publishes an academic-program-to-priority-area mapping at this level of detail.
04 · The Gaps

Where the Federal Portfolio Underinvests

Three measurable asymmetries between MSI degree production and federal STEM investment: demographic access to emerging-tech programs, R&D capacity, and supply vs. workforce demand.

The data: Black students at MSIs earn 9.0% of all STEM bachelor's — but only 1.7% of Advanced Materials, 1.9% of Space Tech, 2.1% of Hypersonics/Gas Turbines, and 2.6% of Advanced Computing. Even within MSIs (where Black enrollment is concentrated), Black students have less institutional access to the highest-leverage emerging-tech programs — programs that often require lab infrastructure, federal research grants, and faculty pipelines that haven't yet been built at scale at these institutions. The federal CHIPS/NSTC priority-funding authorities can address this directly: not just by funding the priority areas, but by building the MSI capacity to host and channel students into them.

Priority areas excluded from this chart: Robotics, Directed Energy, PNT — fewer than 100 MSI bachelor's in 2022. Quantum is excluded because its only CIP (40.0810 Quantum Mechanics) has minimal MSI production. Some priority areas share CIPs (e.g., Hypersonics and Advanced Gas Turbine both rely on aerospace eng), explaining identical %s.

Gap 2 — R&D Capacity

Degree production tells half the story. The other half: research capacity — labs, faculty, federal grants — the infrastructure that turns students into researchers and translates STEM into national-priority innovation. NSF's Higher Education R&D Survey (HERD) tracks this, but only counts institutions that grant bachelor's+ AND spend ≥$150K/yr on R&D.

MSI SHARE OF NATIONAL ACADEMIC R&D, FY2023
$108.68B total higher-ed R&D in NSF HERD-frame institutions (academic R&D only — not all federal STEM funding)
↑ MSI: $9.0B (8.3%)
0% 100%
For comparison: the same 772 MSIs collectively produce 29.9% of all U.S. STEM bachelor's degrees and 21.7% of all U.S. STEM master's + doctorates. The degree-share vs. R&D-share comparison below is a descriptive ratio, not a causal claim. What it does not say: R&D dollars are not allocated proportionally to degree production by any federal policy; this is descriptive math, not a funding-allocation rule.
BACHELOR'S-LEVEL COMPARISON
MSI degree share: 29.9%  ·  R&D share: 8.3%
Ratio: 3.6× — MSIs hold a smaller share of academic R&D capacity than their share of bachelor's-level STEM production. Note: most R&D dollars fund graduate-level research; comparing bach production to R&D dollars compares different educational tiers.
GRADUATE-LEVEL COMPARISON
MSI degree share: 21.7%  ·  R&D share: 8.3%
Ratio: 2.6× — cleaner unit comparison because federal R&D primarily funds graduate research (PhD stipends, post-doc salaries). The gap is smaller at the grad level but still substantial.
HBCU SUBSET (100 institutions combined)
Bach: 1.6% of national share  |  R&D: 0.5%  →  ratio 3.2×
Grad: 0.8% of national share  |  R&D: 0.5%  →  ratio 1.5×
HBCU production and R&D shares are both small (most HBCUs are not research-mission institutions, by Carnegie Classification). The grad-level ratio of 1.5× is the cleanest unit comparison and shows a modest gap. Both ratios reflect descriptive shares, not policy targets.

Gap 3 — Federal STEM Workforce Demand

For each Federal STEM Priority area, the table shows the MSI graduate pipeline contributing to that priority's workforce — graduates from programs (CIPs) whose disciplinary content feeds into the priority's SOC occupations. The National Workforce column shows the total US employment in those occupations (BLS OEWS May 2024) for context.

How counts work here: Each graduate is credited to every federal priority area their academic program could prepare them for. A Computer Science graduate appears in AI/ML, Advanced Computing, Quantum, and Cybersecurity — because CS prepares students for all four. This is a broader view than elsewhere in the dashboard; the goal is to show the full reach of MSI programs into priority workforces. National workforce demand is shown alongside as a reference number — not a denominator — because public federal data doesn't track which specific graduates enter which specific jobs.

06 · Methodology

Methodology, Limits & Sources

Every claim here is traceable to a federal source. The notes below describe the analytical choices and known limitations behind each finding. Methodology, sources, and citation guidance follow.

Five things worth knowing before you cite these numbers

01
The 3.7× & 3.2× ratios compare mismatched units — degrees vs. dollars.
Degree production is a teaching output (counted in students); R&D is a research input (counted in money). Federal R&D isn't allocated proportionally to degree production — it's awarded for research projects. So "MSIs produce 30.7% of degrees but get 8.3% of R&D" implicitly argues that R&D allocation should match teaching output. Some funders accept this principle (capacity-building authorities like NSF HBCU-UP, USDA Capacity); others don't (most NSF and NIH peer-reviewed grants). Better framing for skeptics: R&D per STEM bachelor's grad — HBCUs receive ~31% of the national average ($78K vs $250K per grad). Same math, harder to dismiss.
02
HERD is academic R&D — it's not all federal STEM funding to MSIs.
The "8.3% / 0.5%" numbers are share of academic R&D as surveyed by NSF HERD. HBCUs and other MSIs receive substantial federal STEM funding outside HERD: Title III institutional aid ($364M to HBCUs in FY2024), NSF HBCU-UP (~$33M/yr), HBCU PhD-pathway programs, USDA 1890 Capacity Building Grants, NIH RCMI and BUILD/RISE programs, DoD HBCU/MSI Research and Education Program, and student-side Pell/SEOG. A correct reading: "MSIs are underrepresented in the R&D infrastructure NSF surveys, while receiving substantial support through teaching-side and capacity-building federal authorities."
03
Most HBCUs and many MSIs are teaching-focused — comparing them to R1 R&D infrastructure is a category mismatch.
Roughly 70% of HBCUs are Carnegie-classified as primarily teaching institutions (Bachelor's, Master's, or Special Focus). Their R&D shares look small partly because their institutional missions aren't research-intensive. A peer comparison — HBCUs vs. non-HBCU R2/M1 universities, or HBCUs vs. comparable enrollment-tier institutions — would be more diagnostic than comparison to a HERD total dominated by Johns Hopkins ($3.8B), UCSF ($2.0B), and similar R1s.
04
Federal priority-area counts are a FLOOR, not a ceiling.
The CIP-to-priority alignment is narrow on purpose — only CIPs whose NCES title explicitly names the priority area are counted. A Computer Science grad doing quantum software won't show up in Quantum; a Biology grad working in semiconductors won't show up in Semiconductors. True workforce contribution is higher than these counts suggest, but cannot be measured at national scale without admin wage record linkage (which doesn't exist for STEM-specific occupations).
05
Demographic representation is descriptive — not a causal claim.
A red cell in the demographic × priority heatmap means "this group earns a smaller share of MSI graduates in this priority area than in MSI STEM overall." It is NOT a claim that Black, Hispanic, or AmInd students cannot succeed in these fields, or that MSIs are at fault for the gap. The structural mechanisms (lab infrastructure, faculty pipelines, federal grant access) are visible in the R&D Capacity section, and the federal CHIPS/NSTC capacity-building authorities exist to address them.

Naming these critiques upfront strengthens the analysis. The 30.7% STEM contribution, the 8.3% R&D share, and the priority-area gaps are real, sourced, and verified — but how they're interpreted matters. If you're using this dashboard to make a case, frame it the way the data actually supports.

Methodology & data sources

All data comes from federal sources. The methodology choices below are documented openly so the work can be checked and replicated.

Education supply (graduate counts)
  • NCES IPEDS Completions Survey (2013–2022 collection cycles), accessed via the Urban Institute Education Data Portal API.
  • STEM CIPs defined as the union of NCES STEM CIP series (01, 03, 11, 14, 15, 26, 27, 40, 41) and the DHS STEM Designated Degree Program List (July 2024 update). 513 Core STEM CIPs + 40 Health Research CIPs.
  • Filtered to majornum=1 (first major) to avoid double-counting.
Institutional designations
  • FY 2025 OPE Eligibility Matrix (Department of Education Office of Postsecondary Education, June 2025) — race-conscious framework with explicit HBCU / TCCU / HSI / AANAPISI / PBI / NASNTI / ANNH categories.
  • FY 2026 OPE Eligibility Matrix (June 2026) — race-neutral framework consolidating MSI categories into SIP.
  • HBCU statutory list confirmed against the White House Initiative on HBCUs.
Federal STEM Priorities
  • CHIPS & Science Act of 2022, Public Law 117-167, Section 10387 (Key Technology Focus Areas) — 10 categories established by Congress.
  • NSTC Critical & Emerging Technologies List Update, February 2024 — 18 categories from the National Science & Technology Council interagency process (18 federal departments/agencies).
  • Combined into 19 unified priority areas; Mapping of academic programs and occupations to priority areas is researcher-derived from CHIPS Act text and the NSTC CET 2024 named technology areas. No federal source publishes a CIP-to-priority alignment; the mapping in this dashboard is documented and reusable.
Workforce demand
  • BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (OEWS), May 2024 National File. National cross-industry employment and mean wages by SOC code.
  • Each priority area's "national workforce employment" is the sum of total employment across the priority's mapped SOC codes.
Race/ethnicity classification
  • Standard IPEDS race/ethnicity categories: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, Two or More Races, Nonresident, Race/Ethnicity Unknown.
  • Categories changed in 2010-11 (added "Two or More Races"); all years shown here are post-change.
Known limitations
  • No single supply-vs-demand percentage. Computing "MSIs supply X% of priority workforce demand" would require following individual graduates into specific jobs — data that exists only in a handful of states with mature student-to-workforce tracking systems, and not at the national level. This dashboard shows MSI graduate production and national workforce demand side-by-side without forcing a single ratio.
  • Pipeline contribution is broadly attributed. A Computer Science graduate counts toward AI/ML, Advanced Computing, Quantum, and Cybersecurity workforces — because CS prepares students for all four. The numbers should NOT be read as "this many MSI grads work in each priority"; they reflect the pipeline that contributes to each.
  • Race-disaggregated 10-year trend coverage: 748 of 772 institutions have full 10-year STEM trajectory data; 24 institutions have partial coverage (newly opened, branch campuses, or closed/reopened — list in downloads/01_institution_roster.csv).
  • Pensole Lewis College (Detroit MI) is excluded from quantitative analysis. It relaunched in March 2022 and has not yet entered the IPEDS reporting cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the "MSI pipeline contribution" for Quantum show 26,185 graduates? Does this number represent actual quantum researchers at MSIs?

No. The number represents graduates from programs that contribute to the quantum workforce — Physics, Computer Science, Electrical Engineering, Applied Mathematics. Not all of those graduates work in quantum; most don't. The figure is a pipeline contribution metric, not a head count of quantum researchers. A national supply-vs-demand percentage would require state administrative records linking individual graduates to specific occupations — and this kind of data exists only for a few states, not nationally.

Why use IPEDS 2022 data when 2023 data has been released?

IPEDS collection cycles take 18-24 months to finalize. As of June 2026, the 2022-23 academic year (IPEDS 2023 collection cycle) is the most recent year with finalized, audited completions data including full race/ethnicity breakdowns. Provisional 2023-24 data is available in some federal systems but had not been fully published by Urban Institute's API at the time of this dashboard's publication.

Why isn't Pensole Lewis College in the data even though it's an HBCU?

Pensole Lewis College of Business and Design relaunched in March 2022 after the original Lewis College of Business closed in 2015. The institution has not yet entered the IPEDS reporting cycle (which typically requires 1-2 years of operations before reporting). It is tracked narratively but excluded from quantitative analysis until IPEDS data becomes available.

What's the difference between FY 2025 and FY 2026 designations?

FY 2025 used race-conscious eligibility criteria for federal MSI grants — HSI required ≥25% Hispanic enrollment, AANAPISI required ≥10% AAPI enrollment, etc. Following the December 2025 DOJ legal opinion that race-conscious federal eligibility criteria are unconstitutional, the FY 2026 OPE Eligibility Matrix consolidated those categories into a single race-neutral "Strengthening Institutions Program" (SIP) test based on financial need and institutional capacity. HBCU and TCCU statuses are unaffected because they are defined by federal statute (Higher Education Act and Tribally Controlled Community College Assistance Act), not regulation. This dashboard preserves both frameworks side-by-side.

How did you align IPEDS programs (CIPs) to the CHIPS and NSTC priority areas?

No federal source publishes an academic-program-to-priority-area mapping at this level of detail. The mapping is researcher-built: each academic program code is assigned to a priority area based on its NCES program title matching language from the CHIPS Act (Section 10387) and/or named technology areas in the NSTC CET 2024 list. CIPs may appear in multiple priority areas where they have legitimate dual relevance (e.g., Computer Science 11.0701 feeds AI, Advanced Computing, Quantum, and Cybersecurity workforces). The full alignment table is downloadable above as CSV.

Why are there two Lincoln Universities? Two Glendale Community Colleges?

These are different institutions that share names. Lincoln University of Missouri (UNITID 177940) and Lincoln University of Pennsylvania (UNITID 213598) are both HBCUs founded in the 1850s-60s. Glendale Community College (CA) and Glendale Community College (AZ) are unrelated public community colleges in different states. The dashboard preserves each as a separate row with its correct UNITID and state.

Why is "White" still the largest single race in many MSI race breakdowns?

MSIs are not single-race institutions. An HSI is required to enroll at least 25% Hispanic undergraduates — but that means the remaining 75% can include White, Black, Asian, and other students. Many HSIs in the Southwest and Midwest enroll substantial White populations alongside their majority-Hispanic enrollment. This is a feature of the federal definition, not an error in the data.

Can I cite this dashboard in a peer-reviewed publication?

Yes. Suggested citation: Davis, K.B. (2026). National HBCU & MSI STEM Pipeline Dashboard, v1.0. USC STEM Center, USC Rossier School of Education. All underlying data is downloadable from the Downloads section. Federal data sources (IPEDS, BLS OEWS, OPE Eligibility Matrices, CHIPS Act statutory language, NSTC CET 2024) should be cited directly per your publication's style.
